L1@P0: Historic Building Appraisal
L2@P0: Tin Hau Temple
L3@P0: No. 62 Shui Mei Tsuen, Kam Tin, Yuen Long
L4@P0:  Tin Hau Temple (天后廟) was built in the 10th year of the Qianlong (乾隆,
L5@P0: 1745 ) reign of the Qing (清) dynasty by the Tang (鄧) clan in Shui Mei Tsuen (水
L6@P0: 尾村) of Kam Tin (錦田), Yuen Long. It is for the worship of Tin Hau deity who is
L7@P0: reputed for her protection given to fishermen. The Tangs settled in Kam Tin as far
L8@P0: back as in the Song (宋, 960-1279) dynasty. It was renovated in 1936 and 1968. In
L9@P0: 1968, it was renovated with the help of a monk Fan-bo (芬博) and the villagers.
L10@P0: Historical
L11@P0: Interest
L12@P0:  The temple is a Qing vernacular building having a two-hall-one-courtyard plan
L13@P0: of three bays. It is in symmetrical design with the altar in the middle of the main
L14@P0: hall facing the entrance at the opposite end of the building. The narrow courtyard is
L15@P0: between the entrance and main halls. The main hall is with two side rooms and so
L16@P0: is the entrance hall. The temple was constructed of green bricks with its walls to
L17@P0: support its pitched roofs of timber rafter, purlins and clay tiles. Its walls and roofs
L18@P0: however have been plastered with concrete. Its granite curbs and steps have been
L19@P0: retained. Its main ridges are with geometric mouldings. Wall friezes on its front
L20@P0: façade are with mouldings of floral pattern.
L21@P0: Architectural
L22@P0: Merit
L23@P0:  It is the only Tin Hau temple erected by the Tang clan in Kam Tin to witness
L24@P0: their settlement in the area.
L25@P0: Rarity
L26@P0:  It has little built heritage value as it has been unsympathetically renovated.
L27@P0: Its authenticity has been diminished.
L28@P0: It has group value with other historic buildings including Tang Ching Lok
L29@P0: Ancestral Hall (清樂鄧公祠), Cheung Chun Yuen (長春園) and others nearby.
L30@P0: Built Heritage
L31@P0: Value
L32@P0: Authenticity
L33@P0: Group Value
L34@P0:  The villagers would make regular offerings at the temple on the 1st and 15th
L35@P0: days of every lunar month. They would not have any celebration on Tin Hau
L36@P0: Festival (天后誕) on the 23rd day of the third month. Villagers over 40 would go to
L37@P0: the temple on the 15th day of each first lunar month to have the Dang Wine (燈酒)
L38@P0: of the Dim Dang (點燈) ritual held at the ancestral hall of the village for new born
L39@P0: baby boys of previous year. Tin Hau deity would be invited to the Tai Ping Ching
L40@P0: Chiu (太平清醮) of Kam Tin held once every ten years by taking her statue on a
L41@P0: sedan chair and carried it to an outdoor altar to attend the activities.
L42@P0: Social Value,
L43@P0: & Local Interest

L45@P1: Historic Building Appraisal
L46@P1: Yan Wah Lo
L47@P1: Kwu Tung, Sheung Shui, N.T.
L48@P1:  Yan Wah Lo (仁華廬) is a Hakka (客家) dwelling constructed in the 1920s by
L49@P1: Yeung Ngan-yau (楊雁友) who was an overseas Chinese working in Bandung (萬
L50@P1: 隆) of Indonesia. The building is in Kwu Tung (古洞) between Sheung Shui and
L51@P1: San Tin (新田). It is in the east of Shek Tsai Leng (石仔嶺) of Kwu Tung near the
L52@P1: Kwu Tung Rural Committee’s office building (古洞村公所). Ngan-yau was born in
L53@P1: Meixian (梅縣), the home county of Hakkas, of Guangdong (廣東) province. He
L54@P1: had a grocery in Bandung and when he accumulated a sum, he wanted to build a
L55@P1: house in Meixian. The site he wanted to build a house in Meixian had already been
L56@P1: occupied. Then he chose to settle in Hong Kong due to its geographical advantage
L57@P1: and social stability (moreover, the Dutch colonial government in Indonesia
L58@P1: restricted Chinese from purchasing any farmland and real estates. With the help of a
L59@P1: Hakka native in Yuen Long, bought land in Kwu Tung and built the house. Hakka
L60@P1: artisans for the construction of the house and building materials were from
L61@P1: Meixian. The Hakka house was not completed due to the outbreak of the war in the
L62@P1: mainland. The house he wanted to build was like the Pun Uk (潘屋) in Au Tau (凹
L63@P1: 頭) of Yuen Long. The residence is still owned by the descendents of Ngan-yau in
L64@P1: the corporate ownership of Yeung Ngan Yau Tso (楊雁友祖). It has been rented to
L65@P1: relatives of the Yeungs from the mainland since the 1970s.
L66@P1: Historical
L67@P1: Interest
L68@P1:  The southeast facing residence was intended to be built in a Hakka
L69@P1: two-hall-two-row (兩堂兩橫) style. The right row and the adjoining open courtyard
L70@P1: were not built. It now is Qing (清) vernacular Hakka dwelling having a
L71@P1: two-hall-one-row ( 兩堂一橫 ) plan. The core centre of the building is a
L72@P1: two-hall-one-courtyard middle bay with a side chamber or side room on either side
L73@P1: of the entrance and main halls and the open courtyard. A row of five bedrooms with
L74@P1: a kitchen is on the left separated by a long lane of open courtyard. An entrance is at
L75@P1: the entrance hall and the open lane. The gable wall of the side row of houses is of
L76@P1: the same direction of the two entrances. The building is constructed of green bricks
L77@P1: with its walls to support its pitched roofs of timber rafters, purlins and clay tiles.
L78@P1: The name of the house “仁華廬” ( Yan Wah Lo) is moulded above the entrance
L79@P1: doorway flanked by a couplet “仁端統四, 華祝多三”. The walls are plastered and
L80@P1: painted. The open courtyard is covered with corrugated sheets. A semi-circular
L81@P1: mound of earth called huatouying (花頭塋) or huatai (化胎) was at the back of the
L82@P1: building, a fung shui provision of the Hakkas. The apex of the gable wall of the side
L83@P1: row is of the wood (木) style of the Five Elements (五行).
L84@P1: Architectural
L85@P1: Merit
